recent_posts.title: How Railway fixed AI agent database deletion with guardrails
recent_posts.summary: An AI agent accessed a Railway API token stored on disk and called a volumeDelete mutation, wiping a customer's production database. Railway has since recovered the data and shipped fixes: all deletes now soft-delete for 48 hours (matching the dashboard behavior), backup cascading deletes are delayed, and the team is improving token scoping UX. The post outlines existing guardrails (staged changes, environment RBAC, project deletion grace periods) and new agent-friendly surfaces: a built-in Railway Agent with staged destructive operations, an improved CLI, and a Remote MCP Server at mcp.railway.com that uses short-lived tokens and scoped consent instead of long-lived disk tokens.

recent_posts.title: Better Rails for Agents: A New Remote MCP and Railway Agent in the CLI
recent_posts.summary: Railway is launching two new agent-focused features: a Remote MCP Server at mcp.railway.com and a new `railway agent` command in the CLI. The Remote MCP Server connects any MCP-compatible client (Claude, Cursor, Codex, Copilot, etc.) to Railway via OAuth, with no local install required. The CLI command lets developers interact with Railway's AI agent from the terminal, supporting interactive sessions, one-shot prompts, JSON output, and thread continuation. The MCP surface is intentionally minimal (7 tools), with complex multi-step operations delegated to a `railway-agent` tool to preserve context window efficiency. Architecturally, the MCP server is a route handler inside Railway's existing monolith, reusing auth, permissions, and data infrastructure rather than running as a separate service.

recent_posts.title: Moving Railway's Frontend Off Next.js
recent_posts.summary: Railway migrated its entire production frontend from Next.js to Vite + TanStack Router, completing the switch in just two PRs with zero downtime. The motivation was slow builds (10+ minutes, 6 of which were Next.js), heavy reliance on client-side patterns that didn't fit Next.js's server-first model, and hacky layout workarounds on the Pages Router. The migration was split into two phases: first removing all Next.js-specific APIs, then swapping the framework and generating 200+ routes from the original page tree. Nitro was added as the server layer, consolidating redirects, headers, and caching. Results include builds under 2 minutes, instant dev server startup, type-safe routing, and first-class layouts. Trade-offs include losing built-in image optimization (replaced with Fastly) and ecosystem tools like next-seo (replaced with in-house equivalents). TanStack Start's relative immaturity is acknowledged but accepted.

recent_posts.title: Railway joins Stripe's Agentic Provisioning Protocol for one-command deploys
recent_posts.summary: Railway has partnered with Stripe to implement Stripe's new Agentic Provisioning Protocol (APP), enabling developers to sign up, set up billing, and deploy infrastructure in a single terminal command. Using the Stripe CLI projects plugin, users can provision PostgreSQL, MongoDB, Redis, object storage, and compute services on Railway without ever touching a dashboard. The post explains why MCP alone wasn't sufficient — it handles tool-calling for existing users but can't handle account creation or billing for new users — and positions APP as the missing layer that takes someone from 'Claude just wrote me an app' to 'it's running in production' in one shot. Railway joins PostHog, Supabase, and Vercel in Stripe's developer preview catalog.

recent_posts.title: From registrar to deployed: buying a domain inside Railway
recent_posts.summary: Railway now lets users search, purchase, and configure custom domains entirely within the platform. The feature eliminates the need to switch between tabs and manually copy DNS records. For domains already managed by Cloudflare, a one-click Domain Connect integration automatically adds the required CNAME and TXT records. For new domains, users can search across 250+ TLDs, get AI-powered name suggestions via Claude Haiku, and complete purchase in a few clicks — with DNS and SSL certificates configured automatically. The search is optimized using the Fastly domain research API, Redis caching with stale-while-revalidate, and a WebSocket-based backend. Purchased domains land in a workspace inventory and can be attached to services inline. Intentionally excluded from v1: domain transfers between workspaces, transferring domains out of Railway, and manual DNS record management.

recent_posts.title: A letter to open source builders who deserve more
recent_posts.summary: Railway is launching an open source partner program aimed at helping independent maintainers monetize their projects without going the VC-backed route. Maintainers can publish one-click deployment templates to Railway's marketplace, earn 25% commission on every deployment forever, interact with their user community through a dedicated queue, and access anonymous usage metrics. Railway has already paid out over $1M through its template marketplace and has 30+ partners since September. Planned improvements include a marketplace redesign and enhanced product management tools in Central Station.

recent_posts.title: Networking is a black box, we used eBPF to open it
recent_posts.summary: Railway's network engineer describes building Network Flows, a real-time network observability feature using eBPF to capture packet-level data from containers. The system enriches raw socket buffers with service context, batches 10,000 flows per second per host, and writes roughly one million rows per second to ClickHouse. A key architectural challenge was reducing ClickHouse merge pressure by consolidating ~1,000 independent host writers into three ingestion pipeline writers. The resulting UI visualizes traffic as animated pipes on Railway's service canvas, with pipe width representing throughput and clickable logs exposing kernel-level drop codes. The motivation was twofold: reduce support ticket burden caused by customers misdiagnosing network issues as application bugs, and give developers a top-down view of network problems without requiring tcpdump expertise.

recent_posts.title: Heroku Walked So Railway Can Run
recent_posts.summary: Railway reflects on Heroku's rise and fall as a developer platform, tracing how Heroku's magical git-push deployment experience was undermined by its failure to adopt Docker and open container standards, its structural dependency on AWS infrastructure, and the broader DevOps movement pulling enterprises toward more configurable tooling. Railway positions itself as the spiritual successor to Heroku's developer experience philosophy, built on containers and open standards, running on its own metal rather than reselling another cloud's compute.

recent_posts.title: Railway's new enterprise security features including 2FA, SSO, RBAC and audit logs
recent_posts.summary: Railway has shipped a suite of enterprise security features over the past six months. Key additions include workspace-wide 2FA enforcement, enterprise SSO via SAML 2.0 (Okta, Azure AD, Google Workspace, etc.), three-tier role-based access control (Admin, Member, Deployer), OAuth 2.0/OIDC-based 'Login with Railway' for third-party integrations, comprehensive audit logs exportable via API, automatic Docker image patching with configurable maintenance windows, and a Trust Center at trust.railway.com hosting SOC 2 Type II reports, pen test results, DPA, and subprocessor lists. BAAs for HIPAA and EU DORA documentation are available on enterprise plans.

recent_posts.title: Railway Runs Open Source, Now We're Funding It
recent_posts.summary: Railway is joining the Open Source Pledge and committing $100,000 this quarter to fund open source projects its community relies on. The platform's template marketplace now has 1,800+ templates and has paid out nearly $1 million to template creators. Railway is also expanding its Technology Partner program, allowing open source maintainers to earn up to 25% recurring commission on deployments of their tools, with 31 partners already including Prisma, Drizzle, Redis, and Bun.
